segments.text: Welcome to this practical introduction to retrieval augmented generation. We will build intuition before looking at a small pipeline.
A language model can answer fluently, but its parameters may not contain recent or private facts. Retrieval supplies relevant evidence at question time.
The first stage splits source documents into useful chunks. Chunk size matters because tiny fragments lose context while large fragments dilute relevance.
An embedding model converts every chunk and the user question into vectors. Similar vectors are candidates, not proof that an answer is correct.
Now we retrieve the nearest passages. Metadata filters for date, department, or access permissions can improve both precision and safety.
The prompt tells the model to answer only from retrieved context and cite its evidence. This reduces unsupported claims but does not eliminate them.
Evaluation needs a representative question set. Measure retrieval recall separately from answer faithfulness so a failure can be diagnosed.
Useful production monitoring includes latency, empty retrievals, citation coverage, user feedback, and changes in source freshness.
To recap: prepare documents, embed chunks, retrieve with filters, generate from evidence, and evaluate every stage. Start small and inspect real failures.
